chapters.n: Moroni had finished abridging the Jaredite record (the book of Ether) and expected that to be his last writing. Surprised to still be alive, he keeps hidden from the Lamanites, who would kill him if they found him.

f.w: the account of the people of Jared
I had supposed not to have written more

chapters.n: The Nephite nation has been destroyed, and now the Lamanites are fighting among themselves. Any surviving Nephite is given a terrible choice: deny Jesus Christ or die.

f.w: their wars are exceedingly fierce among themselves

chapters.n: Moroni refuses to deny the Savior, even though it means living as a lonely fugitive. His quiet courage is one of the great examples of faithfulness in all scripture.

f.g: to whatever place; wherever.

chapters.n: So Moroni adds a few more chapters he never planned to write, hoping they will bless his former enemies’ descendants someday. His love for the Lamanites, the very people hunting him, reflects the Savior’s command to love our enemies.

f.w: of worth unto my brethren, the Lamanites

chapters.n: Moroni preserves the words Jesus spoke to the twelve Nephite disciples while laying his hands on each of them. Touch and authority go together: priesthood power is passed on by the laying on of hands.

f.w: the twelve whom he had chosen
as he laid his hands upon them

chapters.n: Jesus called each disciple by name and taught them to pray mightily to the Father in his name, after which they could give the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands. He notes that his apostles in Jerusalem did the same.

f.g: earnest, wholehearted prayer — not a casual or routine request.

f.w: ye shall give the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: This instruction came during Christ’s first visit to the Nephites, spoken privately to the disciples rather than the crowd. Afterward, everyone they laid hands on received the Holy Ghost, showing the promise was fulfilled.
Moroni now records how priesthood offices were conferred. The twelve disciples are here called “elders,” and they ordained others as priests and teachers to serve in the church.
Ordination began with prayer to the Father in Christ’s name, followed by the laying on of hands. Prayer first and then action is a pattern found throughout Restoration scripture.

These are the actual words of ordination. A priest or teacher’s purpose is summed up simply: preach repentance and forgiveness of sins through Jesus Christ, and help people endure in faith to the end.

f.g: forgiveness; the release of a person from the guilt and penalty of sin.

f.w: endurance of faith on his name to the end

chapters.n: Callings were extended according to God’s gifts and will, not human ambition, and ordinations were done by the power of the Holy Ghost. The Restoration likewise teaches that one must be called of God by proper authority.

f.w: according to the gifts and callings of God unto men

chapters.n: Moroni introduces the sacrament, the emblems of Christ’s flesh and blood. Because the disciples followed Christ’s own instructions, Moroni can vouch that this is the correct way to administer it.

f.w: according to the commandments of Christ

chapters.n: The one administering kneels with the whole congregation, a posture of humility and unity. The prayer is offered to the Father in the name of the Son, just as Jesus taught.

This is the prayer on the bread, still used word for word in the Church today. By eating, members remember Christ’s body and witness three commitments: to take his name, always remember him, and keep his commandments. The promised blessing is the constant companionship of his Spirit.

f.g: to make holy; set apart for a sacred purpose.

f.w: willing to take upon them the name of thy Son
always have his Spirit to be with them

chapters.n: Moroni turns to the second part of the sacrament, the cup. Today the Church uses water instead of wine, following later revelation that what matters is doing it with an eye single to God’s glory.

The prayer on the cup focuses on Christ’s blood shed for us. It is shorter than the bread prayer: members witness that they “do always remember him,” and the promise of his Spirit follows. Note that the bread prayer says “always have” his Spirit while this one says “may have.”

f.w: the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them

chapters.n: Moroni explains how people qualified for baptism, including those who would serve as elders, priests, and teachers. Each had to show by their lives that they were ready, not just say so.

f.g: fruit suitable or fitting; evidence in one’s life that matches true repentance.

chapters.n: Baptism required real humility — a broken heart and contrite spirit — and an honest witness to the church that one had repented of all sins. It was a serious covenant, not a casual ceremony.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

f.g: deeply sorry for sin; humbled and teachable.

chapters.n: Candidates also took Christ’s name upon themselves and determined to serve him for the rest of their lives. Baptism marks a beginning, not a finish line.

f.w: took upon them the name of Christ

chapters.n: After baptism and the cleansing power of the Holy Ghost, new members were recorded by name so the church could remember and nourish them. Fellowship, scripture, and prayer kept them on the path, trusting entirely in Christ’s merits.

f.w: relying alone upon the merits of Christ
the author and the finisher of their faith

chapters.n: The church met frequently to fast, pray, and talk with one another about their spiritual well-being. Church was a community that cared for each soul.
They also met often to partake of the sacrament in remembrance of Jesus — the same pattern Latter-day Saints follow in weekly sacrament meeting.
The church guarded its members’ integrity. Serious sin was judged with the testimony of witnesses before the elders, and those who would not repent were removed from membership.
Yet the door always stayed open. Whenever people sincerely repented and asked forgiveness, they were forgiven — a powerful reassurance of the Lord’s patience.

f.g: genuine purpose; meaning it with the whole heart.

chapters.n: Meetings were led by the Spirit: whether someone preached, exhorted, prayed, or sang depended on how the Holy Ghost guided them. The same principle is taught for latter-day meetings.

f.w: conducted by the church after the manner of the workings of the Spirit

f.g: to plead humbly in prayer.

chapters.n: Moroni introduces a sermon his father Mormon once gave in a Nephite synagogue. Its theme — faith, hope, and charity — makes it one of the most treasured discourses in the Book of Mormon.

f.g: a building for worship and teaching; the Nephites used the word much as the Jews of Jesus’ day did.

chapters.n: Mormon begins humbly: he speaks only because God has graciously called him. This is likely before the final wars, when Mormon still led and taught the church.

f.w: the gift of his calling unto me

chapters.n: Mormon addresses faithful church members, calling them “peaceable followers of Christ.” They have enough hope to enter the Lord’s rest now — a peace in this life that continues into heaven.

f.g: disciples whose lives are marked by peace — with God and with others.

chapters.n: Mormon explains how he knows they are faithful: their peaceful way of living with others shows it. Our everyday conduct reveals our discipleship.

f.g: “walk” is a scriptural way of saying one’s manner of life.

chapters.n: He quotes Jesus’ teaching that people are known by their fruits. Good works come from a good heart, just as good fruit comes from a good tree.

f.w: by their works ye shall know them

chapters.n: Mormon teaches that motive matters. A gift or prayer offered without sincere intent brings no spiritual benefit, because God looks on the heart.

f.g: sincere, honest purpose — meaning what one does.

chapters.n: An insincere act is not credited to a person as righteousness. God does not simply tally outward actions; he weighs why we do them.
A gift given grudgingly is, in God’s eyes, as if it had never been given at all. True generosity comes from a willing heart.

f.g: reluctantly; resentfully.

chapters.n: The same applies to prayer. Going through the motions without sincere desire profits nothing, for God does not accept empty words.

f.w: not with real intent of heart

chapters.n: Mormon sums up: a person committed to evil cannot truly do good or give a good gift. The heart must change for the actions to become good.

f.w: a man being evil cannot do that which is good

chapters.n: Using an image from James, Mormon says a bitter spring cannot produce sweet water. No one can serve both Christ and the devil at once; following Christ means choosing a side.

f.w: a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water

chapters.n: Everything good comes from God, and everything evil from the devil, who constantly fights God and tempts people to sin. This sets up the simple test Mormon is about to give.

f.w: all things which are good cometh of God

f.g: lures or tempts; draws someone along by appealing to their desires.

chapters.n: Whatever invites and encourages us to do good, love God, and serve him is inspired by God. This is a key that lets anyone recognize divine influence.

f.w: every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good

chapters.n: Mormon warns against mixing things up — calling evil good or good evil. Confusing the two is a serious spiritual danger.

f.w: judge that which is evil to be of God

chapters.n: God has given us the ability to judge between good and evil, and the way is as clear as the difference between day and night. Discernment is not reserved for the few.

f.w: as the daylight is from the dark night
f.g: a vivid comparison: the difference is meant to be obvious, not subtle.

chapters.n: The “Spirit of Christ” — also called the Light of Christ — is given to every person born into the world. Anything that persuades us to do good and believe in Christ comes from him.

f.w: the Spirit of Christ is given to every man

chapters.n: The opposite is just as clear: anything that leads people to do evil, doubt Christ, or stop serving God comes from the devil. He never persuades anyone to do good.

f.w: he persuadeth no man to do good

chapters.n: Since they know this light of Christ, they must judge carefully and fairly. Echoing Jesus, Mormon reminds them that we will be judged by the standard we use on others.

f.w: with that same judgment which ye judge ye shall also be judged

chapters.n: Mormon pleads with them to search diligently by Christ’s light and to embrace every good thing. Those who do become children of Christ.

f.w: lay hold upon every good thing

chapters.n: Mormon asks a question that turns the sermon toward faith: how can anyone actually take hold of every good thing?
His answer is faith. Mormon now begins the first of his three great themes, explaining how faith connects us to all good.
God, who knows all things, sent angels to announce Christ’s coming long before his birth. Every good thing would come through Christ.

f.w: he sent angels to minister unto the children of men

chapters.n: God also spoke directly to prophets, testifying that Christ would come. All the prophets have borne this witness.
God made good things known in many ways. Because humankind is fallen, no good could reach us at all without Christ.

f.g: various; many different.

chapters.n: Through angels and God’s word, people before Christ’s birth began to have faith in him and so received every good thing. Faith in the coming Christ was the path to salvation in every age.

f.w: every word which proceeded forth out of the mouth of God

chapters.n: After Christ came, people were still saved by faith in his name and became God’s sons and daughters. Mormon quotes Jesus’ promise that good things asked of the Father in faith will be granted.

f.w: they become the sons of God
Whatsoever thing ye shall ask the Father in my name

chapters.n: Mormon asks: now that Christ has ascended to sit at God’s right hand, have miracles stopped? Christ in heaven claims the right to extend mercy to all of us.

f.w: sat down on the right hand of God

chapters.n: Christ fully satisfied the demands of justice and now claims everyone who believes in him. He is our Advocate, pleading our cause with the Father forever.

f.w: answered the ends of the law
f.g: satisfied the purposes and demands of the law of justice.
pleads on behalf of, as a lawyer defends a client.

chapters.n: Mormon answers his own question firmly: no, miracles have not ceased, and angels still minister to people. God’s power did not end with Bible times.

f.w: neither have angels ceased to minister

chapters.n: Angels serve under Christ’s direction and appear to those of strong faith and steady minds. Their ministry is tied to faith and godliness.

f.g: steady, unwavering commitment.

chapters.n: Angels call people to repentance, help fulfill God’s covenants, and teach Christ’s word to chosen servants so they can testify of him. The Restoration itself began with such ministry.

f.g: people God chooses as instruments to carry his message.

f.w: the work of the covenants of the Father

chapters.n: Through these chosen witnesses, everyone else can come to faith in Christ and make room for the Holy Ghost in their hearts. In this way the Father fulfills his covenants.

f.g: the rest of humanity — those who hear through the witnesses.

f.w: that the Holy Ghost may have place in their hearts

chapters.n: Mormon quotes Christ’s promise: those with faith in him can do whatever is needed and right in his eyes. “Expedient in me” means what fits Christ’s will and purposes.

f.g: appropriate, wise, or useful for a purpose.

f.w: ye shall have power to do whatsoever thing is expedient in me

chapters.n: Here is Christ’s universal invitation: everyone, everywhere, should repent, come to him, be baptized, and have faith to be saved. It is a summary of his doctrine.

f.w: Repent all ye ends of the earth

chapters.n: Mormon reasons: if these teachings are true — and God will prove them true at the last day — then how could miracles possibly have ceased?

f.w: with power and great glory at the last day

chapters.n: He presses further: have angels stopped appearing, or the Holy Ghost been withdrawn? Will God ever withhold these while even one person remains to be saved?

f.w: so long as time shall last

chapters.n: No — miracles and angels come by faith. If they ever seem to cease, it is because of unbelief, not because God has changed.

f.w: it is by faith that miracles are wrought
wo be unto the children of men

chapters.n: Since salvation comes only through faith in Christ, the end of miracles would mean the end of faith — and humanity would be as lost as if Christ had never redeemed us.

f.w: as though there had been no redemption made

chapters.n: Mormon expresses confidence in his listeners: their meekness shows they have faith in Christ. Faith is what qualifies someone to belong to his church.

f.w: I judge better things of you

chapters.n: Mormon turns to his second theme, hope, and links it tightly to faith: you cannot have one without the other.
What is the hope? Not wishful thinking, but confident expectation that through Christ’s atonement and resurrection we will be raised to eternal life.

f.w: hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection

chapters.n: Faith and hope always go together. Faith in Christ produces hope, and without faith there is nothing to hope for.
Both faith and hope require meekness and lowliness of heart — teachable humility before God.

f.g: gentle, humble, and willing to submit to God.

chapters.n: God accepts only the meek and humble. Anyone who is humble and testifies by the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ will also have charity — and without charity, a person is nothing.

f.w: confesses by the power of the Holy Ghost that Jesus is the Christ
if he have not charity he is nothing

chapters.n: Mormon describes charity almost word for word as Paul does in 1 Corinthians 13: patient, kind, not envious or proud, not selfish, slow to anger, enduring all things. The near-identical wording suggests a shared source in the Savior’s teaching.

f.g: inflated with pride; arrogant.
is patient; bears with others for a long time.

chapters.n: Charity never fails. Everything else will eventually pass away, so Mormon urges us to hold fast to charity, the greatest gift of all.

f.g: cling tightly; hold fast to.

chapters.n: Mormon defines charity: it is the pure love of Christ — both Christ’s love for us and the Christlike love we come to feel. Whoever has it at the last day will be well.
Charity is a gift we must pray for with all the energy of our hearts. Those filled with it become God’s children, will be like Christ when he appears, and are purified as he is pure.

f.w: pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart
when he shall appear we shall be like him

chapters.n: Moroni includes a letter (epistle) his father Mormon wrote to him shortly after Moroni was called to the ministry. It addresses a false teaching that had crept into the church.

f.g: a formal letter, especially one giving religious instruction.
in this way; as follows.

chapters.n: Mormon opens with a father’s joy that the Lord has called his son into his service. The tenderness between them shines through these letters.
Mormon prays constantly for Moroni, asking that God’s grace will help him stay faithful to the end. Parents praying for children is a pattern throughout scripture.

f.g: “child” here carries the sense of “servant” or “son,” a title also used in the early Christian church.

f.w: endurance of faith on his name to the end

chapters.n: Something has deeply grieved Mormon: arguments have arisen among the church members where Moroni serves.

f.g: heated arguments or disputes, especially over doctrine.

chapters.n: The dispute is over whether little children should be baptized — an issue that also troubled Christians in the Old World for centuries.
Mormon calls infant baptism a “gross error” and asks Moroni to work hard to correct it. That is the whole purpose of his letter.

f.g: a serious, glaring mistake in doctrine.

chapters.n: Rather than rely on his own opinion, Mormon immediately asked the Lord and received an answer by the Holy Ghost. This models how prophets resolve doctrinal questions.

Christ himself answers: he came to call sinners, not the righteous, to repentance. Little children cannot sin, so they are whole; the effects of Adam’s fall have no power over them because of Christ’s atonement.

f.w: the curse of Adam is taken from them in me
the law of circumcision is done away in me

chapters.n: Having received this revelation, Mormon declares that baptizing little children is “solemn mockery” before God — treating a sacred ordinance as if it meant something it does not.

f.g: a serious misuse of something holy, making a show of it in a way that insults its purpose.

chapters.n: Baptism is for those who are accountable and capable of sin. Parents must repent, be baptized, and become humble like their children, so that families can be saved together.

f.w: humble themselves as their little children

chapters.n: Little children need neither repentance nor baptism. Baptism exists for those who repent, as part of keeping the commandments that bring forgiveness of sins.

Children are alive in Christ through his atonement, planned from before the world was made. If unbaptized children were lost, God would be unfair and changeable — and many children have died without baptism.

f.w: alive in Christ, even from the foundation of the world

f.g: someone who plays favorites.

chapters.n: Mormon follows the false idea to its awful conclusion: if baptism were required for children, countless innocent children would be condemned forever.
Mormon speaks strongly: anyone who insists little children need baptism lacks faith, hope, and charity — the very virtues of his sermon in chapter 7 — and is spiritually bound.

f.g: a state of deep spiritual bitterness; gall was a bitter substance.
the chains or bondage of sin.

chapters.n: It would be terrible to believe God saves one child because of a ritual while another child perishes for lack of it. Such a view misrepresents God’s character.
Mormon warns those who twist the Lord’s ways in this manner, and says he speaks boldly with God’s authority, unafraid of human opposition, because perfect love drives out fear.

f.g: to twist or distort from the right meaning.

f.w: perfect love casteth out all fear

chapters.n: Filled with charity, Mormon loves all children equally and perfectly. All of them share in salvation through Christ.
God does not play favorites and does not change. His fairness and constancy are the foundation for trusting him with our children.
Since little children cannot repent, denying them God’s mercy is grave wickedness. They live in Christ purely because of his mercy.
Claiming children need baptism effectively denies Christ’s mercy and treats his atonement and redeeming power as worthless.

f.g: treats as nothing; disregards with contempt.

chapters.n: Mormon repeats his warning with God’s command behind it. Those who teach this error must take heed, or they will face Christ at the judgment with this teaching against them.
Not only little children but also all who lived without God’s law are covered by Christ’s redemption. Those not under condemnation cannot repent, so baptism does nothing for them.

f.w: all they that are without the law

f.g: is of use or benefit.

chapters.n: Baptizing such people mocks God, denies Christ’s mercy and the Spirit’s power, and trusts in “dead works” — empty rituals with no saving power.

f.g: outward acts done without the life of faith or proper purpose.

chapters.n: Repentance is for those who are under condemnation for breaking God’s law — not for innocent children.
Mormon outlines a chain: repentance leads to baptism; baptism, done in faith, fulfills the commandments; and that brings forgiveness of sins.

f.g: the first visible results; in ancient Israel, first fruits were the first part of a harvest offered to God.

chapters.n: The chain continues: forgiveness brings meekness, meekness invites the Holy Ghost, and the Comforter fills us with hope and perfect love. Diligent prayer keeps that love alive until we dwell with God.

f.g: a title of the Holy Ghost; the Greek paraklētos means one who stands by to help.

chapters.n: Mormon turns to the grim war situation. He may soon have to fight the Lamanites, and the Nephites’ pride is bringing about their destruction unless they repent.
He asks Moroni to pray for the Nephites, though he fears the Spirit has stopped striving with them. They are rejecting priesthood authority and denying the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the Spirit hath ceased striving with them

chapters.n: After rejecting so much light, the Nephites will soon perish, as their prophets and the Savior himself had foretold.

f.w: the prophecies which were spoken by the prophets

chapters.n: Mormon signs off with a simple farewell, unsure whether he will write again or see his son. The ordinary goodbye carries the weight of a dying nation.
In a second letter, Mormon assures Moroni he is still alive but warns that the news is painful. The letter is a raw window into the last years of the Nephite nation.

f.g: causing great sorrow or pain.

chapters.n: Mormon reports a lost battle in which three of his officers — Archeantus, Luram, and Emron — and many of his best men were killed. These names appear nowhere else in scripture.

f.g: a fierce, hard-fought battle.
the best, most capable soldiers.

chapters.n: Mormon fears the Lamanites will destroy the Nephites, who refuse to repent and are constantly stirred by Satan to rage against each other.

f.w: Satan stirreth them up continually to anger

chapters.n: Mormon keeps preaching, but nothing works: sharp words make them angry, and gentle words make them harden their hearts. He fears the Spirit has stopped working with them.

f.g: plain, direct, cutting words that call out sin.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord hath ceased striving with them

chapters.n: Their anger is so intense they seem unafraid of death. They have lost love for one another and constantly crave blood and revenge — the opposite of the charity Mormon taught.

f.w: they have lost their love, one towards another

chapters.n: Mormon’s famous counsel: even when people seem hopeless, keep laboring. We have a work to do while in our mortal bodies, to overcome the adversary and find rest in God’s kingdom.

f.g: the mortal body, pictured as a temporary dwelling made of earth.

f.w: if we should cease to labor, we should be brought under condemnation

chapters.n: Mormon relays a report from Amoron: the Lamanites captured men, women, and children at the tower of Sherrizah.
The Lamanites killed the men and then forced the starving women and children to eat their bodies. Mormon records these horrors to show how far a society falls without God.

f.g: barely any water at all.

chapters.n: Yet the Nephites were even worse. At Moriantum they captured Lamanite daughters and robbed them of their chastity and virtue, which Mormon calls most precious of all.
After abusing the women, the Nephites tortured and murdered them and ate their flesh as a show of bravery. Their hearts had become utterly hardened.

f.g: as a sign or proof of courage — showing how twisted their values had become.

chapters.n: Mormon cries out but cannot even finish his sentence — the grief interrupts him. He calls them a people “without civilization.”
In a sad aside, Mormon notes that only a few years earlier these same people had been civilized and delightful. Decline can come swiftly.
Mormon starts again, still unable to complete the thought, overwhelmed by a people who delight in abomination.

f.g: something utterly detestable, especially in God’s sight.

chapters.n: He finishes the question: how could God possibly hold back his judgment from such a people?

f.g: hold back; stop himself from acting.

chapters.n: Mormon’s heart cries woe for his people and asks God to bring judgment and remove their sins from his sight. It is the anguished prayer of a prophet who has run out of options.
Widows and daughters still in Sherrizah were left with nothing: what the Lamanites didn’t take, the Nephite army of Zenephi stole. Many elderly women collapsed and died while searching for food.
Mormon’s own army is weak and cut off from Sherrizah. Those who fled to another Nephite army under Aaron suffered terrible brutality there too.

f.g: between.

chapters.n: Mormon laments that his people have no order or mercy. He is only one man and can no longer make them obey his commands.

f.g: moral corruption; wickedness.

chapters.n: Both sides are equally brutal, sparing no one, delighting in everything except good. The suffering of women and children is beyond words.

f.w: tongue cannot tell, neither can it be written

chapters.n: Mormon stops describing the scene. His people are “past feeling” — so hardened that conscience no longer touches them — and more wicked than the Lamanites.

f.g: spiritually numb; no longer able to feel the promptings of conscience or the Spirit.

chapters.n: Mormon cannot even pray for God to bless such a people; it would be like asking God to approve their wickedness.

f.g: commend them to God’s care and favor.

chapters.n: But he can commend his son to God. He trusts in Christ for Moroni’s salvation and prays Moroni will live to see the Nephites either return to God or be destroyed.

f.w: except they repent and return unto him

chapters.n: If the Nephites perish, it will be like the Jaredites, who destroyed themselves through stubborn hearts and lust for revenge.
Many Nephites have defected to the Lamanites. Mormon asks Moroni to write a little if he survives, and hopes to see him soon to hand over the sacred records.

f.w: I have sacred records that I would deliver up unto thee

chapters.n: Some of the most beloved words in the Book of Mormon: Mormon urges Moroni not to be crushed by grief, but to let Christ lift him up and to keep Christ’s suffering, mercy, and the hope of eternal life always in mind.

f.w: the showing his body unto our fathers

f.g: patient endurance; bearing with others’ faults over a long time.

chapters.n: Mormon closes with a blessing of grace from the Father and from Christ, who sits at God’s right hand until all things are subject to him.

f.w: until all things shall become subject unto him
sitteth on the right hand of his power

chapters.n: Moroni begins his final chapter, addressing the Lamanites. More than 420 years have passed since the sign of Christ’s birth, so this is around AD 421.

f.w: the sign was given of the coming of Christ

chapters.n: Moroni is about to seal up the plates for the last time, but first offers some words of exhortation — earnest encouragement and counsel.

f.g: urgent encouragement to act.

chapters.n: Before asking whether the book is true, readers should remember how merciful God has been to humanity from Adam to their own day, and ponder it deeply. Pondering prepares the heart for revelation.

f.w: remember how merciful the Lord hath been

chapters.n: Moroni’s famous promise: ask God the Father in Christ’s name whether these things are true. If you ask sincerely, with real intent and faith in Christ, he will reveal the truth by the Holy Ghost. Many converts point to this verse as the start of their testimony.

f.g: intending to act on the answer, not merely curious.

f.w: he will manifest the truth of it unto you

chapters.n: The promise reaches beyond the Book of Mormon: by the Holy Ghost we can know the truth of all things. The same Spirit that witnesses of the book can guide us in every search for truth.
Everything good is also just and true, and nothing good denies Christ; rather, it testifies that he lives. This echoes Mormon’s test for discerning good from evil.

f.w: nothing that is good denieth the Christ

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost can witness that Christ lives. Moroni pleads with us not to deny God’s power, which works according to people’s faith and never changes.

f.w: the same today and tomorrow, and forever

chapters.n: Moroni urges readers not to deny the many gifts of the Spirit. They take different forms, but all come from the same God for the benefit of his children.

f.w: deny not the gifts of God

f.g: to benefit or help them.

chapters.n: The list of gifts begins: some receive the ability to teach wisdom — practical, inspired understanding of how to live.

f.g: a spiritual gift of wise teaching; not the same as the health code of D&C 89.

chapters.n: Others are given the gift to teach knowledge — to understand and explain truth clearly — by the same Spirit.
Some receive exceptionally great faith; others the gift of healing. Both come from the same Spirit.
Some are given power to work mighty miracles, as many prophets and apostles have done.
Others receive the gift of prophecy — speaking God’s truth and foretelling events by inspiration.
Some are blessed to see angels and ministering spirits. Moroni himself would later be such a messenger to Joseph Smith.
Others receive the gift of speaking in various tongues — including the ability to learn and speak languages to share the gospel.
Still others can interpret languages and tongues. Together these gifts allow the gospel to reach every nation.
All these gifts come through the Spirit of Christ, given to each person individually as he chooses. No one has every gift, and everyone has some.

f.g: individually; separately to each person.

chapters.n: Moroni reminds us that every good gift comes from Christ — a fitting summary of his father’s teachings.

f.w: every good gift cometh of Christ

chapters.n: Christ is unchanging, so these spiritual gifts will never be taken away as long as the world lasts — unless people lose them through unbelief.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever

chapters.n: Moroni links faith, hope, and charity in a chain: each requires the next. He echoes his father’s great sermon in chapter 7.
Without charity, faith, and hope, no one can be saved in God’s kingdom. All three are essential.

f.g: in no way; not at all.

chapters.n: Without hope, people fall into despair — and despair comes from sin. Hope in Christ is the remedy.
Moroni repeats Christ’s promise to the Nephites: with faith, they can do all that is needful in Christ’s eyes.

f.w: If ye have faith ye can do all things which are expedient unto me

chapters.n: Speaking now to the whole world, Moroni warns that if God’s power and gifts ever disappear from a people, it will be because of their unbelief.

f.w: it shall be because of unbelief

chapters.n: That would be a tragic condition, for no one would do good at all. Anyone who truly does good works by God’s power and gifts.
Those who reject God’s gifts and die without repenting die in their sins. Moroni insists he speaks Christ’s words and tells the truth.

Moroni says we will meet him at God’s judgment bar, where God will ask whether we heeded words written by one “crying from the dead” and “speaking out of the dust” — a description of the Book of Mormon coming forth from the ground.

f.g: the place of judgment, pictured as a courtroom bar.

chapters.n: These words fulfill prophecy. God’s word will “hiss forth” — be called out like a signal — to every generation.

f.g: to whistle or call out as a signal to gather; an image from Isaiah.

chapters.n: Moroni’s confidence is simple: God himself will confirm that what he wrote is true.
His last great invitation: come unto Christ, grasp every good gift, and avoid every evil and unclean thing.

f.w: touch not the evil gift, nor the unclean thing

chapters.n: Moroni draws on Isaiah’s images of Zion awakening, dressing in beautiful garments, and spreading its tent with strengthened stakes. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the gathering of Israel and the growth of the Church.

f.w: arise from the dust, O Jerusalem
strengthen thy stakes and enlarge thy borders

f.g: put to shame; thrown into confusion.

chapters.n: One of the great verses on grace: come to Christ, give up ungodliness, and love God with all your heart, and his grace is enough to make you perfect in him. Perfection is not something we achieve alone but a gift through Christ.

f.w: love God with all your might, mind and strength
then is his grace sufficient for you

chapters.n: Those made perfect in Christ are sanctified — made holy and spotless — through the shedding of his blood, as promised in the Father’s covenant for forgiving sins.

f.g: made holy; cleansed and set apart for God.

chapters.n: Moroni bids farewell, expecting soon to rest in paradise until his resurrection. He will meet us before “the pleasing bar of the great Jehovah” — Christ, the Judge of the living and the dead. About fourteen centuries later he returned as an angel to Joseph Smith.

f.g: Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal name of Jesus Christ.
quick = living; the living and the dead.
